extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American government, civic reformers, and readers interested in state politics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative observations for judging the quality and functioning of U.S. State governments, legislatures, and party systems — including effects of session frequency, party organization, population size, and public opinion on legislative behaviour and reform prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of legislative sessions (biennial/quadrennial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether infrequent legislative sessions (biennial or quadrennial) cause public inconvenience or affect legislative quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes some States report 'None whatever' public inconvenience and even argue less frequent sessions might better subserve public interest; but infrequent sessions can leave members 'rawer' and 'positively more dangerous' when their term includes only one session because they are new to the work. Anti-pattern: adopting infrequency merely to prevent legislatures from meeting and thereby preventing 'bad laws' without addressing root causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment of better citizens vs symptom-focused reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the feasibility and desirability of reforming legislatures by inducing 'good men' to enter and keeping vigilant public opinion, versus treating only symptoms of legislative malady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that reformers often find it too difficult to change legislatures directly and therefore focus on curing symptoms. While some claim the worst outcome is wasting money or foolish experiments, this view neglects erosion of constitutional organs and dangerous social pressures arising from wealth and corporate misuse of public rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative political importance of States
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge how the State's political importance has changed relative to the national government and whether that decline affects citizen engagement and legislative quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although States have grown in wealth and population, they have declined relatively; important issues (trusts, railroads) are national, reducing the imaginative appeal of State matters. Result: State legislatures are left to professionals or 'third-rate men' and do not command the same loyalty they once did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of state population/size on local interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the degree to which large state populations undermine personal acquaintance and civic interest that support effective local government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When States grow large (many with millions), citizens know less of one another and have less personal interest in State affairs; the special advantages of local government (familiarity, interest) largely vanish. Hamilton's suggestion to subdivide large States is mentioned; subdivision trade-offs are noted (e.g., cities vs rural voters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power must be paired with responsibility, interest, and honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether holders of power (voters and legislators) have the corresponding responsibility, direct interest, enlightenment, and sense of honour required to render power salutary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chief lesson: power does not necessarily bring responsibility. For voters there must be direct interest in choosing good men; for legislators, responsibility to voters; for both, enlightenment and honour. Without these, large powers exercised by legislatures are not a guarantee of good behaviour (examples: New York and Pennsylvania as large but poor-quality legislatures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for effective methods to channel public opinion to representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether there exist practical methods by which sound public opinion is brought into efficient action on representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound public opinion may exist, but legislatures of the worst States show the need for mechanisms to make it effective upon representatives who lack personal honour or character to lose. Mere existence of opinion is insufficient without ways to convert it into accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of State parties vs absorption by national parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether State party organizations are independent and focused on State issues or have been absorbed into national parties that swamp State concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author observes three possible relations (independent State parties; State parties influenced by national parties; State organizations as subdivisions of national parties) and concludes national parties have 'engulfed' State parties. Consequence: State parties rarely address State competence issues, local parties lose distinctiveness, and national issues overshadow State business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties should be formed from common state aims/issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate a party's legitimacy and usefulness by whether it is formed around State aims and issues that the State can actually influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural source of a party is a common belief and a common aim about matters the State can do. When a party is formed with reference to matters outside the State's competence (i.e., national issues), it becomes an 'artificial aggregation' and is of little service for most State legislative questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of party cohesion depends on alignment with State issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether party cohesion actually helps the legislature prepare, support, and critique measures relevant to State welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When party platforms do not touch the bulk of State questions, cohesion does not produce legitimate ends (cooperation in preparing measures, support for policies, critical review of opponents' proposals). Parties united by national issues often fail to address State legislative work productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party labels as recruitment incentive vs party-manager domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the claim that party organization attracts better men to State legislatures (as a stepping-stone to national office) against the counter-evidence that party managers, not intellect or character, determine candidacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument for parties: ambition to reach national politics may draw able men into State legislatures. Counterpoint: elections are in the hands of party managers who value party service over intellect or character; experience in legislatures may make politicians proficient in methods but not necessarily better statesmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local and personal bills are outside party lines and occupy most legislative time
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that local/personal bills and local appropriations largely occupy legislatures and are not organized by party issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such bills typically involve members combining across party lines to secure local benefits; party leaders can facilitate passage, and corrupt practices ('rings') are more likely among disreputable members. Party majority status gives district advantages in securing local benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine reform legislation often non-party, but can become party issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess which public measures are considered on merits (e.g., asylum reform, lotteries) versus which tend to become party issues because they mobilize specific electorate groups (e.g., liquor laws, labor hours, railroad attacks, oleomargarine regulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bills improving lunatic asylums or restricting divorce are non-party; liquor or railroad measures may draw partisan involvement because of class/ethnic interest groups (e.g., farmers vs urban beer drinkers) and parties may compete to win such votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-specific third parties can arise around salient local issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the potential for and impact of State-focused third parties or factions formed around particular State issues (e.g., anti-Chinese movement, Readjusters, Grangers, Prohibitionists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such parties sometimes succeed in securing State legislation (railroad regulation, debt readjustment) but often act by influencing the major parties rather than by direct representation; Prohibitionists typically influence policy by pushing regular parties to adopt their doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factions arising from personal rivalries weaken party purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge the risk that intra-party splits driven by leaders' rivalries (personal factions) reduce the substantive principles and dignity of State politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York's Hunkers vs Barnburners, Stalwarts vs Half-breeds — often personal, not principled. Such factions are common and can be more embittered internally than against opponents, diminishing the seriousness of State politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline in dignity and popular engagement in State politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether State politics have become more pacific in method but less serious, more personal, and less likely to stir patriotic interest or public spirit for good State government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical contrast: violent or armed struggles of early republic gave way to electoral battles; while less violent this has not necessarily increased public engagement or concern for State good government; counting votes instead of battles is an improvement but may reduce the intensity of civic devotion to the State.
